To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

AVC dominates BEM in all cases, and AVC requires fewer replications than BEM to achieve the desired level of probability of correct selection for the same number of populations and for the same underlying probability distribution families.

(1) AVC requires no more than BEM in terms of independent observations, and often far fewer, to meet a prespeci fied probability of correct selection, (2) AVC is robust in the number of populations k, and (3) AVC is robust to the distribution family.
AVC is more efficient than BEM for all underlying distribution families, all sample sizes, and all probabilities of correct selection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how to best use the data in a selection problem.
the problem of selecting the best of several populations based on a single observation per population.
the use of all vector comparisons to obtain more information than is obtained using only BEM comparisons.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for all underlying distributions and all sample sizes, AVC dominates BEM.
, if the objective is to correctly select the best system, then AVC is the procedure of choice.
AVC is always better than BEM, in the sense that the number of replications required by AVC is never greater than BEM for any underlying distribution and for any number of populations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AVC is a more efficient use of the data than BEM in multinomial selection and related estimation problems.
AVC is a more efficient procedure for both the selection problem and the estimation of the probability that a system is the best than BEM.
AVC is a better procedure than BEM for the multinomial selection problem, but it is not necessarily a better procedure for the related estimation problem.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for the same amount of data, the AVC procedure can be expected to provide better selection and/or estimation performance than the BEM procedure.
the data in the multinomial selection problem can be used more fully to make better statistical inference.
AVC can be a very attractive alternative to BEM, and that the use of pseudoreplications in this context is a very effective tool.
